lessons.title: Variables
lessons.summary:
Variables store information your program can use later. Think of them like labeled boxes: you give the box a name and put something inside.

There are three ways to create variables:
- `const`: the value never changes (use this by default)
- `let`: the value can change
- `var`: old way, avoid it

When to use what:
Use `const` for everything by default. Switch to `let` only when you know the value will change, like a counter or a loop variable.
lessons.example:
const name = "Daniel"   // never changes
let score = 0           // can change
score = 10              // allowed with let

const age = 20
// age = 21  // ERROR: const cannot be reassigned

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary:
Functions are reusable blocks of code. Instead of writing the same code over and over, you write it once inside a function and call it whenever you need it.

Think of a function like a recipe: you write the steps once, then follow the recipe whenever you want to cook that dish.

Key concepts:
- Parameters are the inputs a function accepts
- Return sends a value back to whoever called the function
- Arrow functions are the modern preferred way to write functions

lessons.title: Array Methods (map, filter, reduce)
lessons.summary:
Array methods let you work with lists of data in a clean and powerful way. The three most important ones are map, filter, and reduce.

Think of arrays like a list of items, and these methods as tools to work with that list.

lessons.title: Async/Await
lessons.summary:
JavaScript is single-threaded: it does one thing at a time. But some things take time, like fetching data from an API. Async/await lets you wait for those things without freezing the whole program.

Think of it like ordering food at a restaurant. You place the order (start the request), do other things while waiting, and when it arrives (data comes back) you eat (use the data).

Key concepts:
- `async` makes a function asynchronous
- `await` pauses until the promise resolves
- Always wrap in try/catch to handle errors

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.summary: Objects store related data together using key-value pairs. Think of an object like a profile card: it holds multiple pieces of information about one thing.

lessons.title: Destructuring
lessons.summary:
Destructuring lets you pull values out of arrays and objects quickly, without writing multiple lines of code.

Think of it like unpacking a suitcase: instead of taking out each item one by one, you unpack everything at once.

lessons.title: Template Literals
lessons.summary: Template literals let you embed variables directly inside strings. Instead of using + to combine strings, you use backticks and ${} to insert values cleanly.
lessons.example:
const name = "Daniel"
const age = 20

// Old way (messy)
"Hello, " + name + "! You are " + age + " years old."

// Template literal (clean)
`Hello, ${name}! You are ${age} years old.`

// Multi-line strings
const message = `
  Welcome back, ${name}.
  Your account is active.
`

lessons.title: Error Handling (try/catch)
lessons.summary:
Things go wrong in code: APIs fail, data is missing, users enter bad input. Error handling lets you catch those problems and respond gracefully instead of crashing.

Key concepts:
- `try`: run the risky code
- `catch`: handle the error if something goes wrong
- `finally`: always runs, whether success or failure

lessons.title: Basic Types (string, number, boolean)
lessons.summary:
TypeScript adds types to JavaScript. Types tell the computer what kind of data a variable holds, catching mistakes before your code runs.

Think of types like labels on containers: "this box holds numbers" prevents you from accidentally putting text in it.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.summary: Interfaces define the shape of an object: what properties it must have and what types they should be. They're like a contract your data must follow.

lessons.title: Type Aliases
lessons.summary: Type aliases create a custom name for a type. Similar to interfaces but more flexible: you can use them for primitives, unions, and more.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summary:
Generics let you write reusable code that works with different types. Instead of writing the same function for strings and for numbers, you write it once with a generic type.

Think of generics like a template: fill in the type when you use it.

lessons.title: Union Types
lessons.summary: Union types let a variable hold more than one type. Use the | symbol to say "this can be A or B."

lessons.title: Utility Types (Partial, Omit, Record)
lessons.summary: Utility types are built-in TypeScript helpers that transform existing types. They save you from rewriting types by hand.

lessons.title: Semantic HTML
lessons.summary:
Semantic HTML uses tags that describe what they contain. Instead of using `<div>` for everything, you use meaningful tags that tell browsers and screen readers what each section is.

This improves accessibility, SEO, and makes your code easier to read.
lessons.example:
```html
...
Home About
...
...
``` **Common semantic tags:** - `header`: top of page or section - `nav`: navigation links - `main`: main content - `section`: grouped content - `article`: standalone content - `footer`: bottom of page

lessons.title: Flexbox
lessons.summary:
Flexbox makes it easy to lay out elements in a row or column. The parent becomes a flex container and controls how children are arranged.

Think of it like a shelf: you decide if items go left-to-right or top-to-bottom, how spaced out they are, and how they align.

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.summary:
CSS Grid is for two-dimensional layouts: rows AND columns at the same time. Perfect for page layouts, dashboards, and card grids.

Flexbox is one direction. Grid is both directions.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.summary: Responsive design makes your website look good on all screen sizes: phone, tablet, and desktop. You use media queries to apply different styles at different screen widths.

lessons.title: CSS Variables
lessons.summary:
CSS variables (custom properties) let you store a value once and reuse it everywhere. Change the variable in one place and every element using it updates.

Define them on :root so the whole page can use them, then read them with var().

lessons.title: Selectors and Specificity
lessons.summary:
Selectors choose which elements a CSS rule applies to. When two rules target the same element, specificity decides which one wins.

Order from weakest to strongest: element (p) < class (.card) < id (#header) < inline style. If specificity is equal, the rule written last wins.
lessons.example:
p { color: black; } /* element: weakest */ .note { color: blue; } /* class: beats element */ #intro { color: red; } /* id: beats class */ /*

-> red */ /* Combining selectors */ .card h2 { font-size: 20px; } /* h2 inside .card */ .btn:hover { opacity: 0.8; } /* pseudo-class */ input[type="email"] { width: 100%; } /* attribute */

lessons.title: Variables and Data Types
lessons.summary: Python variables don't need a type declaration: Python figures it out automatically. This is called dynamic typing.
lessons.example:
name = "Daniel"        # string
age = 20               # integer
height = 5.11          # float
is_active = True       # boolean
skills = ["JS", "Python"]  # list
user = {"name": "Daniel"}  # dictionary

# f-strings (like template literals)
print(f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.")

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.summary: Functions in Python use the `def` keyword and indentation instead of curly braces.
lessons.example:
def greet(name):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

# With default parameter
def greet(name="stranger"):
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

greet("Daniel")   # "Hello, Daniel!"
greet()           # "Hello, stranger!"

# Lambda (like arrow functions)
double = lambda x: x * 2
double(5)  # 10

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Python loops are clean and readable. The `for` loop works great with lists and ranges.
lessons.example:
# For loop
for i in range(5):
    print(i)  # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4

# Loop through a list
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

# While loop
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

# List comprehension (powerful shortcut)
squares = [x ** 2 for x in range(10)]

lessons.title: Conditionals
lessons.summary: Python uses `if`, `elif`, and `else`. Indentation is how Python knows what's inside each block. No curly braces needed.

lessons.title: Lists and Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Lists are ordered collections. Dictionaries store key-value pairs. These are Python's most used data structures.
lessons.example:
# List
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
fruits.append("mango")
fruits.remove("apple")
fruits[0]  # "banana"

# Dictionary
user = {
    "name": "Daniel",
    "age": 20,
    "skills": ["Python", "JavaScript"]
}
user["name"]          # "Daniel"
user["city"] = "Dallas"  # add new key
user.get("email", "N/A") # safe access with default

lessons.title: File I/O
lessons.summary:
File I/O means reading from and writing to files. Python's open() gives you a file object, and using it with 'with' closes the file automatically when you're done.

Modes: 'r' read, 'w' write (overwrites), 'a' append.
lessons.example:
# Write (creates or overwrites the file)
with open("notes.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("First line\n")

# Append
with open("notes.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("Second line\n")

# Read the whole file
with open("notes.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())

# Read line by line
with open("notes.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        print(line.strip())

lessons.title: Exception Handling
lessons.summary:
Exceptions are errors that happen while your program runs. try/except lets you catch them so your program doesn't crash.

Catch specific errors (like ValueError) instead of everything, and use finally for code that must always run.

lessons.title: SELECT queries
lessons.summary: SELECT is how you read data from a database. It's the most used SQL command: you'll write it constantly.

lessons.title: WHERE and filtering
lessons.summary: WHERE filters rows so a query only returns the ones that match a condition. Combine conditions with AND / OR, and use operators like =, >, LIKE, IN, and BETWEEN.

lessons.title: JOINs
lessons.summary: JOINs combine data from multiple tables. The most common is INNER JOIN: it returns rows where there's a match in both tables.
lessons.example:
-- Tables: users and orders
-- Each order has a user_id

-- INNER JOIN: only matching rows
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
INNER JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all users, even without orders
SELECT users.name, orders.total
FROM users
LEFT JOIN orders ON users.id = orders.user_id;

lessons.title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
lessons.summary: These are the write operations in SQL: creating, changing, and removing data.
lessons.example:
-- INSERT: add new row
INSERT INTO users (name, email, age)
VALUES ('Daniel', 'daniel@example.com', 20);

-- UPDATE: change existing row
UPDATE users
SET age = 21
WHERE id = 1;

-- DELETE: remove row
DELETE FROM users
WHERE id = 1;

-- CAREFUL: DELETE without WHERE deletes everything!

lessons.title: Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG)
lessons.summary:
Aggregate functions take many rows and return one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.

Pair them with GROUP BY to get one result per group, and use HAVING to filter those groups.

lessons.title: Indexes
lessons.summary:
An index is like the index in the back of a book: it helps the database find rows quickly without scanning the whole table.

Add indexes on columns you search or join on often. They speed up reads but make writes slightly slower, so don't index everything.

lessons.title: Components
lessons.summary:
Components are the building blocks of React. Every piece of UI is a component: a button, a card, a nav bar. They're just functions that return JSX.

Build small components and combine them into bigger ones. Like LEGO blocks.

lessons.title: Props
lessons.summary: Props are how a parent component passes data to a child component. They work like function arguments and are read-only: the child should never change them.

lessons.title: useState
lessons.summary: useState lets your component remember and update data. When state changes, React automatically re-renders the component to show the new data.

lessons.title: useEffect
lessons.summary: useEffect runs code after the component renders. Use it for fetching data, setting up subscriptions, or anything that needs to happen after the UI appears.

lessons.title: Event Handlers
lessons.summary: Event handlers are functions that run when the user does something: clicks, types, submits a form. Pass the function itself (onClick={handleClick}), not the result of calling it.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering
lessons.summary: Conditional rendering means showing different UI depending on a condition. Use && to show something or nothing, and a ternary (? :) to choose between two options.

lessons.title: Lists and Keys
lessons.summary:
Use .map() to turn an array into a list of elements. Every item needs a unique key so React can track which items changed.

Use a stable id from your data as the key. Avoid using the array index if the list can be reordered.

lessons.title: Fetching Data
lessons.summary: To load data from an API in a client component, fetch it inside useEffect and store the result in state. Track loading and error states so the user always sees something useful.

lessons.title: File-Based Routing
lessons.summary: In Next.js you don't set up a router manually. Just create a file and it becomes a page automatically. The file name and folder structure define the URL.
lessons.example:
app/
  page.tsx              →  /
  about/
    page.tsx            →  /about
  blog/
    page.tsx            →  /blog
    [id]/
      page.tsx          →  /blog/123
  api/
    users/
      route.ts          →  /api/users

lessons.title: App Router
lessons.summary:
The App Router uses folders inside app/ to create routes. A folder becomes a URL segment, and a page.tsx file inside it is what shows on that URL.

layout.tsx wraps pages and stays on screen between navigations. Components are Server Components by default; add "use client" when you need state or events.
lessons.example:
app/ layout.tsx -> wraps every page page.tsx -> / about/ page.tsx -> /about blog/ page.tsx -> /blog [slug]/ page.tsx -> /blog/my-post // app/about/page.tsx export default function AboutPage() { return

About

}

lessons.title: Server vs Client Components
lessons.summary: Next.js has two types of components. Server components run on the server and are faster, so use them by default. Client components run in the browser and are needed for interactivity.

lessons.title: API Routes
lessons.summary: Route handlers let you build backend endpoints inside your Next.js app. Create a route.ts file and export functions named after HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.).

lessons.title: Dynamic Routes
lessons.summary: Dynamic routes use square brackets in a folder name, like [id], to match any value in that part of the URL. The value is passed to your page through params.

lessons.title: Image Optimization
lessons.summary: Next.js's <Image> component automatically resizes, compresses, and lazy-loads images. It also prevents layout shift because you give it a width and height.

lessons.title: Deployment to Vercel
lessons.summary: Vercel is made by the Next.js team, so deploying is almost zero setup. Connect your GitHub repo and every push to main deploys automatically, while every pull request gets a preview URL.
lessons.example:
# Option 1: Dashboard
# vercel.com -> New Project -> Import GitHub repo -> Deploy

# Option 2: CLI
npm i -g vercel
vercel          # preview deploy
vercel --prod   # production deploy

# Add secrets in Project Settings -> Environment Variables
# NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix = visible in the browser

lessons.title: What is Node.js
lessons.summary: Node.js lets you run JavaScript on the server, outside of the browser. Before Node.js, JavaScript only worked in browsers. Now you can use the same language for frontend and backend.

lessons.title: HTTP Module
lessons.summary: Node.js has a built-in HTTP module for creating servers. This is what Express builds on top of.

lessons.title: npm and packages
lessons.summary:
npm is Node's package manager. It installs libraries other people wrote and tracks them in package.json.

dependencies are needed to run the app; devDependencies are only needed while developing (like testing tools). Never commit node_modules.
lessons.example:
npm init -y                # create package.json
npm install express        # add a dependency
npm install -D vitest      # add a dev dependency
npm uninstall express      # remove a package
npm install                # install everything in package.json

// package.json scripts
"scripts": {
  "dev": "next dev",
  "test": "vitest"
}

npm run dev

lessons.title: File System (fs)
lessons.summary: The fs module lets Node read, write, and manage files. Use the promise version (fs/promises) with async/await so you don't block the server.

lessons.title: Environment Variables
lessons.summary:
Environment variables store config and secrets (API keys, database URLs) outside your code. Node reads them from process.env.

Keep them in a .env file and add .env to .gitignore so secrets never reach GitHub.
lessons.example:
# .env
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/app

// server.js (Node 20+ can load .env with --env-file)
// node --env-file=.env server.js
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000
console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL)

# .gitignore
.env

lessons.title: Setting up a server
lessons.summary: Express makes building servers much simpler than the raw Node.js HTTP module. Less code, cleaner syntax, same result.

lessons.title: Routes (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
lessons.summary: Routes define how your server responds to different requests. Each route has a method (GET, POST, etc.) and a path.

lessons.title: Middleware
lessons.summary:
Middleware are functions that run between the request arriving and the response being sent. They can read or change the request, end it early, or call next() to pass it on.

Use them for logging, parsing JSON, auth checks, and more.

lessons.title: CORS
lessons.summary:
Browsers block requests from one origin (like localhost:5173) to a different one (like localhost:3000) unless the server allows it. That rule is CORS.

The cors package adds the headers that tell the browser which origins are allowed.

lessons.title: Error Handling
lessons.summary: Express has a special error-handling middleware with four arguments (err, req, res, next). Put it after all your routes so any error ends up in one place and returns a clean response.

lessons.title: REST API design
lessons.summary:
REST APIs use URLs for resources (nouns) and HTTP methods for actions (verbs). Use plural nouns, and return the right status codes.

GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes.
lessons.example:
GET    /api/users       -> list users       200
GET    /api/users/42    -> one user         200 / 404
POST   /api/users       -> create user      201
PATCH  /api/users/42    -> update user      200
DELETE /api/users/42    -> delete user      204

// Bad:  POST /api/createUser
// Good: POST /api/users

app.get("/api/users", listUsers)
app.post("/api/users", createUser)
app.delete("/api/users/:id", deleteUser)

lessons.title: Utility Classes
lessons.summary:
Tailwind CSS uses utility classes: small, single-purpose classes you combine directly in your HTML. No writing custom CSS files.

Instead of writing `.button { background: blue; padding: 8px 16px; }` you write `bg-blue-500 px-4 py-2` directly on the element.
lessons.example:
Card Title

Card description here.

lessons.title: Responsive Design
lessons.summary: Tailwind makes responsive design easy with breakpoint prefixes. Add `md:` or `lg:` before any class to apply it only at that screen size.
lessons.example:
```html
Left
Right
Home About
``` **Breakpoints:** - `sm:`: 640px and up - `md:`: 768px and up - `lg:`: 1024px and up - `xl:`: 1280px and up

lessons.title: Flexbox and Grid utilities
lessons.summary:
Tailwind has utility classes for Flexbox and Grid so you can build layouts without writing CSS.

Use flex for one direction (a row or a column). Use grid for rows and columns together. Add breakpoints like md: to change the layout on bigger screens.
lessons.example:
Logo
Links
...
Card
Card
Card

lessons.title: Custom colors and spacing
lessons.summary:
You can extend Tailwind's default theme with your own colors and spacing. In Tailwind v4 you define them in CSS with @theme, and they become classes automatically.

For one-off values, use square brackets like w-[350px].

lessons.title: Dark mode
lessons.summary: Add the dark: prefix to any class to apply it only in dark mode. By default it follows the user's system setting.
lessons.example:
Hello

Works in light and dark.

/* Toggle manually with a .dark class instead (Tailwind v4) */ @custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *)); // JS toggle document.documentElement.classList.toggle("dark")

lessons.title: Git Basics (add, commit, push)
lessons.summary:
Git tracks changes to your code over time. Think of it like a save system: you can always go back to any previous version of your project.

The three commands you use every day:
lessons.example:
```bash
# Stage changes (tell Git what to include)
git add .

# Save a snapshot with a message
git commit -m "feat: add login page"

# Send to GitHub
git push origin main

# See what changed
git status

# See commit history
git log --oneline
```

**Good commit message format:**
- `feat:`: new feature
- `fix:`: bug fix
- `docs:`: documentation
- `refactor:`: code cleanup

lessons.title: Branching
lessons.summary: Branches let you work on new features without touching the main code. Create a branch, do your work, then merge it back when ready.
lessons.example:
# Create and switch to new branch
git checkout -b feature/login-page

# See all branches
git branch

# Switch between branches
git checkout main

# Merge branch into main
git merge feature/login-page

# Delete branch after merging
git branch -d feature/login-page

lessons.title: Merging and Pull Requests
lessons.summary:
Merging combines the work from one branch into another. On teams you usually merge through a Pull Request so someone can review the changes first.

If two branches changed the same lines, Git can't decide on its own and you get a merge conflict to fix by hand.
lessons.example:
# Merge a branch locally
git checkout main
git pull
git merge feature/login

# Conflict markers look like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const title = "Home"
=======
const title = "Welcome"
>>>>>>> feature/login

# Fix the file, then:
git add .
git commit

# After a PR is merged on GitHub
git checkout main
git pull
git branch -d feature/login

lessons.title: .gitignore
lessons.summary: A .gitignore file lists files and folders Git should not track. Use it for dependencies, build output, logs, and secrets like .env.
lessons.example:
# .gitignore
node_modules/
.next/
dist/
.env
.env.local
*.log
.DS_Store

# Already committed a file by mistake? Stop tracking it:
git rm --cached .env

lessons.title: Git history and logs
lessons.summary: Git keeps a full history of every commit. git log shows what changed, who changed it, and when, which is useful for finding when a bug was introduced.
lessons.example:
git log                    # full history
git log --oneline          # one line per commit
git log --oneline --graph  # show branches visually
git log -p app/page.tsx    # changes to one file
git show 3f2ef2e           # details of one commit
git diff                   # unstaged changes
git blame app/page.tsx     # who last changed each line

lessons.title: Basic Commands (pwd, ls, cd, mkdir, rm)
lessons.summary: The terminal lets you control your computer with text commands. Every developer uses it daily: running servers, installing packages, managing files.
lessons.example:
pwd              # show current directory
ls               # list files
ls -la           # list all files including hidden

cd projects      # go into folder
cd ..            # go back one level
cd ~             # go to home directory

mkdir my-app     # create folder
touch index.js   # create file
rm file.txt      # delete file
rm -rf folder/   # delete folder (careful!)

cat file.txt     # read file contents
echo "hello"     # print text

lessons.title: File permissions (chmod)
lessons.summary:
Every file has permissions for read (r), write (w), and execute (x), set separately for the owner, the group, and everyone else. chmod changes them.

Numbers add up: read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. So 7 = rwx, 6 = rw-, 4 = r--.
lessons.example:
ls -l
# -rw-r--r--  1 daniel staff  script.sh
#  owner group others

chmod +x script.sh     # make it executable
./script.sh

chmod 755 script.sh    # rwx r-x r-x
chmod 644 notes.txt    # rw- r-- r--
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519  # private key: only you

lessons.title: Grep and Find
lessons.summary: Grep searches inside files for text. Find searches for files by name. Both are powerful tools for navigating large codebases.
lessons.example:
# Search for text inside files
grep "TODO" file.js
grep -r "TODO" .           # search all files recursively
grep -r "useState" src/    # find all useState usages

# Find files by name
find . -name "*.tsx"       # all TypeScript React files
find . -name "index.js"    # find index.js anywhere
find . -type f -name "*.env" # find env files

lessons.title: SSH basics
lessons.summary:
SSH lets you securely connect to another computer, like a server, from your terminal. It's also how you can push to GitHub without typing a password.

You make a key pair: the private key stays on your machine, and the public key goes on the server or GitHub.
lessons.example:
# Create a key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com"

# Copy the public key (add it in GitHub -> Settings -> SSH keys)
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Test the GitHub connection
ssh -T git@github.com

# Connect to a server
ssh user@203.0.113.10

lessons.title: Environment variables
lessons.summary: Environment variables are named values your shell and programs can read, like PATH or HOME. You can set your own for a single session or save them in your shell config so they're always there.
lessons.example:
echo $HOME            # print a variable
echo $PATH
env                   # list all

export API_KEY=abc123 # set for this session
echo $API_KEY

# Make it permanent (zsh)
echo 'export API_KEY=abc123' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

# Set just for one command
PORT=4000 npm run dev

lessons.title: Shortcuts
lessons.summary: Keyboard shortcuts save a lot of time. Learn a few at a time until they become habit. (Mac shown; on Windows use Ctrl instead of Cmd.)
lessons.example:
Cmd + P           Quick open a file
Cmd + Shift + P   Command palette
Cmd + D           Select next match
Option + Up/Down  Move line up/down
Shift + Option + Down  Duplicate line
Cmd + /           Toggle comment
Cmd + B           Toggle sidebar
Ctrl + `          Toggle terminal
F2                Rename symbol everywhere
F12               Go to definition

lessons.title: Extensions
lessons.summary:
Extensions add features to VS Code: linting, formatting, language support, and more. Install them from the Extensions panel (Cmd + Shift + X).

Start with a few useful ones; too many can slow the editor down.
lessons.example:
Popular for web dev:
- ESLint             -> shows code problems
- Prettier           -> auto-formats code
- Tailwind CSS IntelliSense -> class autocomplete
- GitLens            -> see who changed each line
- Error Lens         -> errors shown inline

// settings.json: format on save
{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode"
}

lessons.title: Debugging
lessons.summary:
The debugger lets you pause your code on a line (a breakpoint) and inspect variables step by step, instead of adding console.log everywhere.

Click left of a line number to add a breakpoint, then start debugging with F5.

lessons.title: Terminal integration
lessons.summary: VS Code has a built-in terminal, so you can run commands without leaving the editor. You can open several terminals at once, like one for the dev server and one for git.
lessons.example:
Ctrl + `             Toggle terminal
Ctrl + Shift + `     New terminal
Cmd + \              Split terminal

# Typical setup
Terminal 1: npm run dev
Terminal 2: git status / git commit

# Open the current folder in VS Code from any terminal
code .

lessons.title: Git integration
lessons.summary: The Source Control panel (Cmd + Shift + G) lets you stage, commit, and push without typing git commands. Changed files show up with M (modified), U (untracked), or D (deleted).
lessons.example:
1. Open Source Control (Cmd + Shift + G)
2. Click + next to a file to stage it
3. Type a commit message
4. Click Commit
5. Click Sync / Push

Click a changed file to see a side-by-side diff.
The branch name in the bottom-left corner lets you switch branches.

lessons.title: Creating repositories
lessons.summary: A repository (repo) is a project folder that GitHub stores along with its full history. You can create it on GitHub first, or start locally and push it up.
lessons.example:
# Start locally, then push to a new GitHub repo
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit"
git branch -M main
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/my-app.git
git push -u origin main

# Or with the GitHub CLI
gh repo create my-app --public --source=. --push

# Copy an existing repo
git clone https://github.com/username/my-app.git

lessons.title: Pull Requests
lessons.summary:
Pull Requests (PRs) are how you propose changes to a codebase. Instead of pushing straight to main, you push a branch and open a PR so others can review it before it's merged.

This is how most professional teams work. Writing "Closes #5" in the description closes the issue automatically when the PR is merged.
lessons.example:
# 1. Create a branch
git checkout -b feature/new-button

# 2. Make changes and commit
git add .
git commit -m "Add new button component"

# 3. Push the branch
git push -u origin feature/new-button

# 4. Open the PR (or click "Compare & pull request" on GitHub)
gh pr create --title "Add new button" --body "Closes #5"

# 5. After review, merge it
gh pr merge

lessons.title: GitHub Actions (CI/CD)
lessons.summary: GitHub Actions automates tasks when you push code. The most common use is CI/CD: automatically running tests and deploying your app when you push to main.
lessons.example:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:

jobs:

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm run build

lessons.title: README best practices
lessons.summary:
The README is the first thing people see in your repo. A good one says what the project is, how to run it, and what it looks like.

Add a screenshot or live link. Recruiters often skim READMEs.

lessons.title: GitHub Pages
lessons.summary: GitHub Pages hosts static websites (HTML, CSS, JS) for free, straight from a repo. It's good for portfolios and simple sites. It can't run a backend server.
lessons.example:
1. Push your site (with an index.html) to GitHub
2. Repo -> Settings -> Pages
3. Source: Deploy from a branch
4. Branch: main, folder: / (root)
5. Save

Your site goes live at:
https://username.github.io/repo-name/

# Repo named username.github.io -> https://username.github.io/

lessons.title: HTTP Methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
lessons.summary: REST APIs use HTTP methods to define what action you want to perform. Think of them like verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes.

lessons.title: Status Codes (200, 400, 401, 404, 500)
lessons.summary:
Every API response includes a status code that tells you if the request succeeded or failed.

**Common codes:**
```
200: OK (success)
201: Created (new resource made)
400: Bad Request (you sent wrong data)
401: Unauthorized (not logged in)
403: Forbidden (logged in but no permission)
404: Not Found (resource doesn't exist)
500: Internal Server Error (something broke on the server)
```

lessons.title: Request and Response
lessons.summary:
Every API call is a request and a response. The client sends a request (method, URL, headers, sometimes a body), and the server sends back a response (status code, headers, body).

Status codes: 2xx success, 4xx client mistake, 5xx server error.

lessons.title: Headers and Body
lessons.summary:
Headers are extra information about a request or response, like the content type or an auth token. The body is the actual data being sent, usually JSON.

GET requests normally have no body; POST, PUT, and PATCH usually do.

lessons.title: JSON format
lessons.summary:
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard format APIs use to send data. It looks like a JS object, but keys must use double quotes and it can't hold functions.

JSON.stringify turns an object into a JSON string; JSON.parse turns it back.
lessons.example:
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Daniel",
  "isStudent": true,
  "skills": ["React", "Node"],
  "address": { "city": "Dallas" },
  "phone": null
}

const user = { name: "Daniel", age: 20 }
const text = JSON.stringify(user)   // '{"name":"Daniel","age":20}'
const back = JSON.parse(text)       // object again

lessons.title: How JWT works
lessons.summary:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is how apps handle authentication. After logging in, the server gives you a token. You send that token with every future request to prove who you are.

Think of it like a concert wristband: show your ID once at the door, get a wristband, then flash the wristband everywhere else.

**The flow:**
```
1. User logs in with email + password
2. Server verifies credentials
3. Server creates a JWT token
4. Client stores the token
5. Every request includes the token in the header
6. Server verifies the token on each request
```

lessons.title: Register and Login flow
lessons.summary:
Register: hash the password and save the user. Login: find the user, check the password against the hash, and if it matches, send back a JWT.

Never store plain-text passwords. Use bcrypt to hash them.

lessons.title: Token verification
lessons.summary: When a request comes in with a JWT, the server checks that it was signed with your secret and hasn't expired. If it's valid, you can trust the user info inside it.

lessons.title: Protected routes
lessons.summary: A protected route only works for logged-in users. Use middleware that verifies the token first: valid means continue, missing or invalid means return 401.

lessons.title: Refresh tokens
lessons.summary:
Access tokens should expire quickly (like 15 minutes) for safety. A refresh token lasts longer and is used only to get a new access token, so the user doesn't have to log in again.

Store the refresh token in an httpOnly cookie so JavaScript can't read it.

lessons.title: Setting up API key
lessons.summary: To use Gemini, get a free API key from Google AI Studio and keep it in an environment variable. Only use it on the server. Never put it in frontend code or commit it to GitHub.
lessons.example:
1. Go to aistudio.google.com
2. Click "Get API key" -> Create API key
3. Copy it

# .env.local
GEMINI_API_KEY=your_key_here

# .gitignore
.env*

npm install @google/genai

lessons.title: Making requests
lessons.summary: Use the official SDK to send a prompt and get a response. Run it on the server (an API route) so your key stays secret.

lessons.title: Prompt design
lessons.summary: Clear prompts get better results. Give the model a role, the task, any context, and the exact output format you want. Examples help a lot.

lessons.title: Handling responses
lessons.summary: AI responses can fail or come back in an unexpected shape. Wrap calls in try/catch, check that you actually got text, and validate JSON before using it.

lessons.title: Use cases
lessons.summary: Common ways to use an AI API in a web app: summarizing text, chatbots, generating quiz questions, classifying or tagging content, and pulling structured data out of messy text.

lessons.title: Fetch API
lessons.summary:
fetch() is the built-in way to make HTTP requests in the browser and in Node. It returns a Promise with a Response; call .json() to read the body.

fetch doesn't throw on 404 or 500, so check res.ok.

lessons.title: Async/Await with APIs
lessons.summary:
async/await makes async code read top to bottom like normal code. Mark the function async, then await each Promise.

Use Promise.all to run independent requests at the same time instead of one after another.

lessons.title: Error handling
lessons.summary: API calls can fail because of network issues, bad status codes, or bad data. Use try/catch, check res.ok, and show the user a friendly message instead of a blank screen.

lessons.title: Environment variables for keys
lessons.summary: Keep API keys in environment variables, not in your code. In Next.js, only variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ reach the browser. Anything secret should NOT have that prefix and should only be used on the server.
lessons.example:
# .env.local
GEMINI_API_KEY=secret123                       # server only
NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=https://myapp.vercel.app  # safe in browser

// Server (API route / server component) - OK
const key = process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY

// Client component - this is undefined, which is good
const key = process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY

# Remember to add the same variables in Vercel -> Settings -> Environment Variables

lessons.title: CORS
lessons.summary:
If your frontend calls an API on a different domain and the browser shows a CORS error, the API server hasn't allowed your origin. It's a browser rule, so the fix is on the server, not in your fetch call.

If you don't control the API, call it from your own backend or Next.js API route instead.

lessons.title: Sliding Window
lessons.summary:
Sliding Window is a technique for working with arrays or strings. Instead of using nested loops (slow), you maintain a window that slides through the data (fast).

Use it when you need to find a subarray or substring that meets some condition.

lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.summary:
Two Pointers uses two variables moving through data, usually one from each end. It replaces nested loops with a single loop, making your code much faster.

Use it on sorted arrays when looking for pairs or comparing from both sides.

lessons.title: Hash Maps
lessons.summary: Hash Maps (objects in JavaScript) store key-value pairs for O(1) lookup: instant access regardless of size. Use them for counting, grouping, and caching.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.summary:
Binary search finds a value in a sorted array by checking the middle and throwing away half the array each step. It's O(log n): about 20 steps for a million items.

The array must be sorted first.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.summary: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem. Every recursive function needs a base case that stops it; otherwise it runs forever.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: An array is an ordered list of values, accessed by index starting at 0. Reading by index is fast (O(1)); searching for a value means checking items one by one (O(n)).
lessons.example:
const nums = [10, 20, 30]

nums[0]            // 10
nums.length        // 3
nums.push(40)      // add to end
nums.pop()         // remove from end
nums.includes(20)  // true

const doubled = nums.map((n) => n * 2)       // [20, 40, 60]
const big = nums.filter((n) => n > 15)       // [20, 30]
const total = nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) // 60

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.summary: Objects store data as key-value pairs. Looking up a value by its key is fast, which makes objects (and Map) great for counting things or quick lookups.

lessons.title: Linked Lists (concept)
lessons.summary: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. Adding or removing at the start is fast, but finding an item means walking the chain from the beginning.

lessons.title: Stacks and Queues
lessons.summary:
A stack is Last In, First Out (LIFO), like a stack of plates: you add and remove from the top. A queue is First In, First Out (FIFO), like a line at a store.

Stacks power undo buttons and the call stack; queues are used for tasks waiting their turn.

lessons.title: Trees (concept)
lessons.summary:
A tree is a structure of nodes where each node can have children, starting from one root. The HTML DOM and your file system are both trees.

In a binary search tree, smaller values go left and bigger values go right, which makes searching fast.

lessons.title: DRY principle
lessons.summary:
DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself. If you write the same code more than once, extract it into a function or component.

Repeated code means if you need to change something, you have to change it in multiple places, which leads to bugs.

lessons.title: Single Responsibility
lessons.summary:
Each function or component should do one thing. If you need the word "and" to describe what it does, it probably should be split up.

Small, focused pieces are easier to read, test, and reuse.

lessons.title: Meaningful variable names
lessons.summary: Good names explain what something is without needing a comment. Use full words, name booleans like questions (isLoading, hasError), and name functions with verbs (getUser, calculateTotal).

lessons.title: Code comments
lessons.summary:
Good code explains what it does through clear names. Comments should explain why: a business rule, a workaround, or something surprising.

Delete commented-out code. Git already remembers it.

lessons.title: Refactoring
lessons.summary:
Refactoring means improving how code is written without changing what it does. Rename unclear variables, remove duplication, and split long functions, in small steps.

Having tests makes refactoring safe, because they tell you if you broke something.

lessons.title: Single Responsibility
lessons.summary: The S in SOLID: a class or module should have only one reason to change. If a class handles both business logic and saving to the database, a change to either one forces you to touch it.

lessons.title: Open/Closed
lessons.summary: The O in SOLID: code should be open for extension but closed for modification. Add new behavior by adding new code, not by editing working code and stacking more if/else statements.

lessons.title: Liskov Substitution
lessons.summary: The L in SOLID: if B extends A, you should be able to use B anywhere you use A without breaking things. A subclass shouldn't remove or break behavior its parent promises.

lessons.title: Interface Segregation
lessons.summary: The I in SOLID: don't force code to depend on methods it doesn't use. Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one big one.

lessons.title: Dependency Inversion
lessons.summary: The D in SOLID: high-level code should depend on abstractions (interfaces), not concrete details. Pass dependencies in instead of creating them inside, so they're easy to swap or fake in tests.

lessons.title: What is CI/CD
lessons.summary:
CI (Continuous Integration) automatically checks every push, for example by running tests and lint. CD (Continuous Deployment) automatically ships the code once the checks pass.

The goal: catch bugs early and deploy without manual steps.
lessons.example:
Developer pushes code
        |
        v
CI: install -> lint -> test -> build
        |
   passes? -- no --> fix and push again
        |
       yes
        v
CD: deploy to production

lessons.title: Writing a workflow file
lessons.summary: GitHub Actions workflows are written in YAML files stored in `.github/workflows/`. They define what happens when you push code, open a PR, or on a schedule.
lessons.example:
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test-and-build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v3

      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm install

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build
        run: npm run build

lessons.title: Running tests automatically
lessons.summary: GitHub Actions runs workflows defined in YAML files inside .github/workflows/. A simple workflow installs dependencies and runs your tests on every push and pull request.
lessons.example:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

lessons.title: Deploying on push
lessons.summary:
You can have a workflow deploy your app when code is pushed to main. Store secrets (like deploy tokens) in the repo's Settings > Secrets and read them with secrets.NAME.

Vercel and Render can also auto-deploy on push without any workflow file.
lessons.example:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - name: Trigger Render deploy
        run: curl -X POST "${{ secrets.RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK }}"

lessons.title: Status badges
lessons.summary: A status badge shows whether your workflow is passing, right in your README. It tells visitors (and recruiters) that your project is tested.
lessons.example:
<!-- README.md -->
![CI](https://github.com/USERNAME/REPO/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)

<!-- Example -->
![CI](https://github.com/Dtzul04/GuideBooks/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)

Tip: in GitHub go to Actions -> pick the workflow -> "..." -> Create status badge

lessons.title: What is Docker
lessons.summary:
Docker packages your app with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config) into a container. The container runs the same way on your laptop, a teammate's machine, or a server.

It solves the "works on my machine" problem.
lessons.example:
docker --version
docker run hello-world          # run a test container

docker run -p 8080:80 nginx     # run a web server
# open http://localhost:8080

docker ps                       # running containers
docker stop <container-id>

lessons.title: Images and Containers
lessons.summary: An image is a read-only template, like a recipe. A container is a running instance of that image, like the meal you cooked. You can start many containers from one image.
lessons.example:
docker pull node:20           # download an image
docker images                 # list images

docker run -it node:20 node   # start a container from it
docker ps -a                  # list all containers
docker stop my-app
docker rm my-app              # delete a container
docker rmi node:20            # delete an image

lessons.title: Dockerfile basics
lessons.summary:
A Dockerfile is a list of steps for building an image: pick a base image, copy your code, install dependencies, and say how to start the app.

Copy package.json first so Docker can cache the install step.
lessons.example:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]

# Build and run
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-app

lessons.title: Docker Compose concept
lessons.summary: Docker Compose runs several containers together from one file, like your app plus a database. One command starts everything with the right settings and connections.
lessons.example:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:secret@db:5432/app
    depends_on:
      - db

  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: app

docker compose up -d   # start everything
docker compose down    # stop everything

lessons.title: Why containerization matters
lessons.summary:
Containers give everyone the same environment, so there are fewer setup headaches and "works on my machine" bugs. New teammates can run the app with one command, and the same image goes from development to production.

They're lighter than virtual machines because they share the host's operating system.
lessons.example:
Without containers:
- "Install Node 20, Postgres 16, set these 8 env vars..."
- Different versions on every machine
- Bugs that only happen in production

With containers:
- docker compose up
- Same versions everywhere
- Easy to scale: run more copies of the container

lessons.title: Vercel (frontend)
lessons.summary: Vercel is the easiest way to deploy Next.js and React apps. Connect your GitHub repo and every push to main deploys automatically. Every pull request also gets its own preview URL.
lessons.example:
1. Go to vercel.com
2. Click "New Project"
3. Import your GitHub repo
4. Build settings are usually auto-detected
5. Add environment variables
6. Click Deploy

Every push to main -> production deploy
Every PR           -> preview deploy

lessons.title: Render (backend)
lessons.summary:
Render hosts backends like Express APIs, plus databases and background workers. Connect your repo, set the build and start commands, and it redeploys on every push.

On the free tier the server sleeps after inactivity, so the first request can be slow.
lessons.example:
1. render.com -> New -> Web Service
2. Connect your GitHub repo
3. Build command:  npm install
4. Start command:  node server.js
5. Add environment variables (DATABASE_URL, JWT_SECRET...)
6. Create Web Service

// Use the port Render gives you
const port = process.env.PORT || 3000
app.listen(port)

lessons.title: Environment variables in production
lessons.summary: Environment variables store sensitive data like API keys and database URLs outside your code. Never hardcode secrets, and never commit them to GitHub.
lessons.example:
# .env file (never commit this)
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@host/db
JWT_SECRET=your-secret-key
GEMINI_API_KEY=your-api-key

# .env.example (commit this: it shows what variables are needed)
DATABASE_URL=
JWT_SECRET=
GEMINI_API_KEY=
```

```js

// Access in Next.js (must prefix with NEXT_PUBLIC_ for client)
const apiUrl = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL

lessons.title: Custom domains
lessons.summary:
A custom domain (like myname.dev) replaces the default URL your host gives you. Buy a domain from a registrar, add it in your hosting dashboard, then update the DNS records it tells you to.

DNS changes can take a few minutes to a few hours to spread.
lessons.example:
1. Buy a domain (Namecheap, Cloudflare, Porkbun...)
2. Vercel -> Project -> Settings -> Domains -> Add "myname.dev"
3. In your registrar's DNS settings add what Vercel shows, e.g.:

   Type    Name   Value
   A       @      76.76.21.21
   CNAME   www    cname.vercel-dns.com

4. Wait for DNS to update. HTTPS is set up automatically.

lessons.title: Monitoring basics
lessons.summary: Monitoring tells you when your live app breaks or slows down, ideally before users notice. Start with logs, error tracking (like Sentry), and uptime checks.
lessons.example:
What to watch:
- Errors        -> Sentry, or your host's logs
- Uptime        -> UptimeRobot pings your site every few minutes
- Performance   -> Vercel Analytics / Speed Insights
- Logs          -> Vercel or Render dashboard

// Log useful info, not secrets
console.error("Payment failed", { orderId, status: res.status })

lessons.title: What is PostgreSQL
lessons.summary:
PostgreSQL is a powerful open-source relational database. Data is stored in tables with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet, but much more powerful and queryable.

You've already used it in Magnifit and FinderDallas through Supabase.

lessons.title: Tables and schemas
lessons.summary:
A table stores one kind of thing (users, posts), and each column has a data type. A schema is the overall design: tables, columns, and how they connect through keys.

A primary key uniquely identifies each row; a foreign key points to a row in another table.

lessons.title: CRUD operations
lessons.summary:
CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four basic things you do with data. In SQL they map to INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

Always use WHERE with UPDATE and DELETE, or you'll change every row.

lessons.title: Relationships (one-to-many)
lessons.summary: Tables can be related to each other. A user can have many posts. A post belongs to one user. This is called a one-to-many relationship.
lessons.example:
-- Users table
CREATE TABLE users (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);

-- Posts table (belongs to a user)
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  content TEXT,
  user_id INTEGER REFERENCES users(id),  -- foreign key
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT NOW()
);

-- Get all posts with author name
SELECT posts.title, users.name AS author
FROM posts
INNER JOIN users ON posts.user_id = users.id;

lessons.title: Supabase setup
lessons.summary: Supabase gives you a hosted PostgreSQL database plus auth and an auto-generated API. Create a project, add tables in the dashboard, and query them from your app with the supabase-js client.

lessons.title: SELECT and filtering
lessons.summary: SELECT picks which columns to return, WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts, and LIMIT caps how many rows come back. Select only the columns you need instead of * in real apps.

lessons.title: JOINs (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT)
lessons.summary:
JOINs combine rows from two tables using a related column.

INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, with NULL where there's no match. RIGHT JOIN is the same idea but keeps every row from the right table.
lessons.example:
-- Users who have posts
SELECT users.name, posts.title
FROM users
INNER JOIN posts ON posts.user_id = users.id;

-- All users, even ones without posts (title will be NULL)
SELECT users.name, posts.title
FROM users
LEFT JOIN posts ON posts.user_id = users.id;

-- Short aliases
SELECT u.name, COUNT(p.id) AS post_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN posts p ON p.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.name;

lessons.title: Aggregate functions
lessons.summary:
Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) turn many rows into a single value. Use GROUP BY to get one result per group and HAVING to filter the groups.

WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters after.

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.summary: A subquery is a query inside another query. Use one when you need a value or list from one query in order to run another, like "products priced above average".
lessons.example:
-- Products more expensive than average
SELECT name, price
FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);

-- Users who have placed at least one order
SELECT name FROM users
WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders);

-- Subquery as a temporary table
SELECT category, max_price
FROM (
  SELECT category, MAX(price) AS max_price
  FROM products
  GROUP BY category
) AS top_prices;

lessons.title: Indexes and performance
lessons.summary:
Indexes make lookups fast, so the database doesn't have to scan every row. Add them on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY.

Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see if a query is slow and whether it uses an index.

lessons.title: What is NoSQL
lessons.summary:
MongoDB is a NoSQL database: instead of tables and rows, it stores documents (like JSON objects) in collections. More flexible than SQL but less structured.

When to use SQL vs NoSQL:
- SQL (PostgreSQL) → structured data, relationships, financial data
- NoSQL (MongoDB) → flexible data, rapid prototyping, content

lessons.title: Documents and Collections
lessons.summary: MongoDB stores data as documents (JSON-like objects) inside collections (groups of documents). There's no fixed schema, so documents in one collection can have different fields, and you can nest related data.

lessons.title: CRUD in MongoDB
lessons.summary: MongoDB CRUD uses methods on a collection: insertOne, find, updateOne, deleteOne. Filters are objects that describe which documents to match.

lessons.title: When to use SQL vs NoSQL
lessons.summary:
SQL databases (PostgreSQL) use strict tables and relationships, which is great when data is connected and must stay consistent, like orders, payments, and users.

NoSQL databases (MongoDB) use flexible documents, which is great when the data shape changes often or is naturally nested, like logs, content, or prototypes.
lessons.example:
Choose SQL (PostgreSQL) when:
- Data has clear relationships (users -> orders -> items)
- You need JOINs and strong consistency
- Example: e-commerce, banking, most web apps

Choose NoSQL (MongoDB) when:
- The data shape changes often
- Data is nested / self-contained
- Example: content feeds, logs, chat messages

Not sure? PostgreSQL is a safe default.

lessons.title: Mongoose basics
lessons.summary: Mongoose is a library that adds schemas, validation, and simple methods on top of MongoDB in Node. You define a schema, create a model from it, then use the model to read and write data.
